title: Back-to-School To-Do List #2: Establish Burning Questions
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart opens with a premise learned at the Lake Michigan Writing Project's Summer Institute: the most effective professional development grows out of the questions a teacher is currently wrestling with, the ones that burn. He then uses that method on himself, laying out four questions for the coming year, three of them about how argument is taught. The first is that teaching delivery through PVLEGS improved how students spoke but not what they said, illustrated by a debater who claimed the atomic bomb was bad because it created smog; he responds with self-check questions on academic vocabulary, evidence-claim links and source reliability. The second locates a 'listening bottleneck': students hear each other but rarely analyze and challenge weak arguments, which he attributes mainly to gaps in his own teaching. The third is an honest tension over research, which he has left out of his approach because reading, writing and speaking come first, yet which cannot be ignored in the Google era. The last question turns to sustaining encouragement through the grinding stretches of the school year.
points: The organizing claim is that a teacher's own burning questions, pursued with time, research and practice, are the most effective professional development available.

His smog anecdote shows that explicit instruction in delivery improved how students spoke while the substance stayed weak, so he adds pre-speaking checks on vocabulary accuracy and whether evidence actually supports the claim.
He argues that discipline-specific vocabulary is less forgiving than ELA vocabulary because a technical process usually has exactly one correct word, so the thesaurus is no help.

He diagnoses a 'listening bottleneck' in classroom debate - students attend to peers but do not dismantle their arguments - and takes responsibility for it as a gap in his teaching rather than theirs.
On research he names the tension rather than resolving it: reading, writing and argument should be mastered first, yet research is itself a form of all three and cannot be skipped.
quotes: It seems super simple, but this question put into words an instinct that I had felt even from early on in my career: the most effective professional development possible, for me, comes from the questions I'm currently wrestling with as a teacher, particularly those that burn — the ones that hit me repeatedly throughout the day, the ones I just know I can get closer to answering with a little more time, a little more research, a little more practice.

Yet while their delivery improved, their content was often weak. In others words, they got better at how to speak (go figure –when you teach them how to do that, they get better!), but they still fumbled around a bit with what to say.

This is hugely important in the content areas because, unlike in ELA, discipline-specific vocab means something specific — you can't bust out the thesaurus nearly as often when you're writing or speaking in the content areas because there's just one word for a technical thing or process. Thank you to Justin of Owens Valley Unified School District for clarifying that for me.

So I need to get better at teaching listening. It's like there's this listening bottleneck in my kids — they hear each other, they pay attention, but they don't consistently do that plus analyze one another's arguments. And they can.
At the same time, I realize that research is a kind of reading, a kind of writing, a kind of speaking and arguing. In the Google era, you can't not teach kids to do research.
So how do we keep our heads and hearts focused on the important stuff? How do we combat stress, both in ourselves and in others?
